content_metadata.description: An in-depth analysis of a presentation video regarding the "Frank R. Lautenberg Chemical Safety for the 21st Century Act" by Jeff Morris.

qAndA.answer: PBT chemicals are Persistent, Bioaccumulative, and Toxic chemicals that pose risks to human health and the ecosystem.
qAndA.question: What are PBT chemicals?

qAndA.answer: Under the old TSCA, new chemicals could enter the market without EPA action. The new law requires the EPA to make an affirmative determination on new chemicals before they can be introduced into the marketplace.
qAndA.question: What was the main difference between the old and new TSCA regarding new chemical substances entering the marketplace?

qAndA.answer: The new law allows the EPA to collect up to $25 million in annual user fees.
qAndA.question: What is the maximum amount of annual user fees that can be collected to support the implementation of the new law?

qAndA.answer: If the EPA's assessment indicates a chemical is safe, state provisions regarding that chemical are preempted.
qAndA.question: What happens to state laws if the EPA determines that a chemical is safe?

qAndA.answer: The mood is neutral, informative, and content, with a focus on the presentation of factual information supported by straightforward visuals.
qAndA.question: What is the mood of the video and how do the visuals and audio contribute to it?

scenes.contextualRelevance: Explanation of the "Frank R. Lautenberg Chemical Safety for the 21st Century Act."

narrativeProgression.description: Jeff Morris begins his presentation on the new law.
Explains the EPA's new mandatory duty to prioritize and assess chemicals for safety.
Highlights that chemicals will be assessed against a risk-based safety standard.
Explains the mandatory regulatory action required when the EPA identifies an unreasonable risk.
Discusses the prioritization process for existing chemicals.
Explains what a risk evaluation entails under the new law.
Details the timeline and process for risk evaluation.
Explains how chemical manufacturers can request risk evaluations.
Discusses the changes for new chemicals entering the marketplace.
Describes the special provisions for PBT chemicals.
Mentions the law's focus on preemption of state laws.

changes that the law brought to us and they are significant.
So now we have a mandatory duty to prioritize and assess those chemicals for safety.
And we have to do that against a risk-based standard.
If the EPA does identify an unreasonable risk associated with its evaluation of an existing
chemical substance, it must then move directly to regulatory action to address those risks.
And that's where cost benefit, balancing, impact on the economy, substitutes, etc. come
into play.
Finally, for this slide, an expanded authority to acquire information on chemicals.
The first thing we have to do is do a prioritization exercise to take those existing substances,
those thousands of however many there are and I'll get to that in a minute and come
up with a process for prioritizing them to identify which substances might be high and low
for risk evaluation.
If we identify a chemical as a high priority for risk evaluation, we must move directly
then to conduct that risk evaluation.
We have three years to do it.
One starting point is to fulfill another provision of the law which is to identify an active inventory
of chemical substances.
So whatever that number is of active substances, that becomes the universe on which we'll do
this prioritization exercise to identify those chemicals that will be candidates for risk
evaluation.
A risk evaluation means more than just an assessment of the risk.
It also means a determination about whether that chemical presents an unreasonable risk for
the conditions of use of that chemical.
Now the law requires us to do evaluations on the conditions of use and generally speaking,
we believe that that means most if not all of the identifiable uses of that chemical
substance.
Then three and a half years we have to be able to do in 20 substances a year for risk evaluation
and as we complete one, another one needs to come into the program through that prioritization
process that I mentioned.
All of these issues related to conditions of use, unreasonable risk, reasonably available
information to connect to risk evaluation.
There's a lot of discussion going on with what those terms mean and how they would affect
an evaluation of an existing chemical.
A lot of this is going to play out in the doing obviously and these first 10 I think will
be our proving ground as to how we work with those concepts articulated in the law.
How we work reasonableness into the evaluation to make the determination based solely on
the assessment and risk based criteria is something that we're all going to have to work
through.
Certainly we have benchmarks that we've used for decades for risk, cancer and non-cancer.
So we'll have to work these out through the first 10.
But if in those first 10 should we identify risk of concern, then we'll have to move
right to risk management and those cost factors will begin to come into play in how we address
those risks.
We've got two years to do risk management action after I haven't identified those risks
in the evaluation.
The work plan isn't the only place that is a source of chemicals for risk evaluation.
Chemical manufacturers can request a risk evaluation of a chemical as well.
If that chemical is one of the work plan chemicals, then the law says that the manufacturer should
pay half of the cost of the risk evaluation.
If it's not on the work plan, they pay the full cost.
For new chemicals, the changes were equally profound in that now for a new chemical substance
during our pre-manufacture review, we must make an affirmative determination as to whether
that chemical substance presents an unreasonable risk.
I've outlined here where essentially for considerations that or determinations that the agency might

The first is the will present.
If we have information that suggests that the chemical substance will present an unreasonable

under Section 5E to basically state that if the company wants to commercialize this
substance, then we're going to need additional information prior to commercialization.
Make a finding of may present unreasonable risk.
We made this previously.
What's changed though now is that under the new law, we would make a determination for
known and reasonably foreseen uses.
That means to us, as we're interpreting the law now, is that the known uses are in
the pre-manufactured notice.
The company says we intend to commercialize this substance for these uses, those two us
are the known uses.
The reasonably foreseen uses, as we're interpreting that now, is if there are uses associated
with a close analog to this chemical, a chemical that seems to be one that's closely
related and could likely be used in the same way as the PMN substance, and there are
uses there that are not on the PMN form, then we would have to make our determination not
only on the uses that are in the PMN form, but also on those reasonably foreseen uses.
And finally, there's the finding of not likely to present unreasonable risk.
Finding not likely doesn't say safe, but it's with the language it was in the law.

Making that affirmative finding is a big change.

youtube_description: Jeff Morris of the US EPA provides an overview of The Frank R. Lautenberg Chemical Safety for the 21st Century Act - the amendment of the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA). Among others Jeff Morris addresses the prioritization of chemicals for risk evaluation, the risk-based safety standard, TSCA work plan, manufacturer requested assessments, costs, new chemicals – affirmative finding and persistent, bioaccumulative and toxic chemicals
